sn11.1:2.1: The gods (_deva_) stem from Proto Indo-European _*dyew_, “shining, sky, heavens” (English “day” is a false friend), while the titans (_asura_) are the negative form of Proto Indo-European _*sóh₂wl̥_, “sun”, i.e. “sunless, night”. As the day vanquishes the dark of night each dawn, the gods defeat the titans. Victory is sweet but short-lived, for soon follows dusk, at which the titans prevail and plunge the world into darkness once more.
sn11.1:4.4: _Disa_ is imperative of _disati_ (“show”) in the sense “render, bestow, confer”.
sn11.1:7.1: The Chinese texts at both SA2 43 (活) and SA 1114 (生) appears to support _jīvati_ rather than _jīyati_. Bingenheimer at SA2 43 has, “Have you ever seen or heard of someone who, without effort, attains happiness in life?” Both Chinese texts have more lines than the Pali; given that the Pali has five lines, it seems likely the text has suffered loss. I translate according to what I guess the meaning to have been.
sn11.1:8.2: This is a tricky construction. The idiom _idha kho taṁ, bhikkhave, sobhetha_ occurs several times, always in the same context: someone is said to have some quality, and the mendicants are encouraged to have it even more so. The preceding clause usually includes _hi nāma_, suggesting a dependent clause ([sn11.2:8.2](), [sn11.4:13.2](), [sn35.103:5.7](), [pli-tv-kd16:6.4.2](), [pli-tv-kd5:4.3.1]()). _Sobhetha_ is second plural optative in the sense “you all can (out)shine or excel”.
